nameStory: The American smoketree gets its dreamy name from the wispy, smoke-like clouds that appear after its flowers fade. What looks like puffs of pink-gray smoke are actually clusters of tiny hairs growing on the spent flower stalks, creating an ethereal haze around the tree that can last for weeks.
description: American smoketree is a rare, deciduous shrub or small tree that can grow up to 33 feet tall and 26 feet wide, forming a conical shape. It's famous for producing some of the most brilliant scarlet fall color of any tree in North America. In summer, it creates its signature "smoky" effect with clusters of pink-gray, hair-like structures that follow its small flowers, giving the entire plant a misty, cloud-like appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves up to 5 inches long with a distinctive inverted egg shape - broader at the tip than at the base. They feel smooth to the touch and turn an absolutely stunning scarlet red in fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink-gray flowers appear in loose, airy clusters called panicles during summer. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees, so you'll need both nearby for the full smoky effect.

idTips.label: Smoke Effect
idTips.description: The famous "smoke" appears after flowering as wispy clusters of fine, hair-like structures on the flower stalks. These create a hazy, pink-gray cloud effect that can cover much of the tree and feels soft and feathery to the touch.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: When cut or broken, the inner wood reveals a bright, sunny yellow heartwood that's quite distinctive and almost glows against the darker outer bark.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a neat, conical shape as it grows, typically remaining shrub-like but capable of becoming a small tree. Branches have a somewhat open, airy appearance even without leaves.

habitat: American smoketree is extremely rare in New England, with only 2 recorded observations in the region. When found, it's typically in cultivated settings like botanical gardens or as a prized landscape specimen, since it's not native to New England but rather to scattered locations in the southeastern and south-central United States.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, showing their distinctive oval, inverted egg shape. Young foliage has a fresh green color and smooth texture.
seasonality.summer: Small pink-gray flowers appear in loose clusters, followed by the spectacular smoky effect as hair-like structures develop on spent flower stalks. The smoky haze can persist for weeks.
seasonality.fall: Produces some of the most intense scarlet fall color of any tree - the leaves turn brilliant red that seems to glow in sunlight. This is often the best time to spot one from a distance.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the conical growth habit and branching pattern. Any remaining smoky seed clusters may persist, looking like wispy gray tufts against the sky.

funFact: The bright yellow heartwood of American smoketree was historically so prized that it was called "chittamwood" and used to make a yellow dye - but you'd have to cut down this rare beauty to see it, which makes it one of nature's best-kept secrets!
confusionNotes: In New England, American smoketree is most likely to be confused with its more common European cousin, smokebush (Cotinus coggygria), which is widely planted in gardens. The main difference is that smokebush typically stays smaller and more shrub-like, while American smoketree can become a proper small tree with more intense fall color.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "American" smoketree, this species is not native to New England at all - it's naturally found in scattered locations across the southeastern and south-central United States. Any specimens in New England are cultivated plants, making them quite special to encounter.
compareHints: American smoketree differs from the more common smokebush (Cotinus coggygria) by growing larger and more tree-like rather than staying shrubby, and by producing more intense fall color. American smoketree also has slightly larger leaves and can reach greater heights, making it the giant of the smoketree world.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The only close relative in New England is the native American smoketree, which is much rarer and has larger, more distinctly egg-shaped leaves.
